title: LangGraph: checkpointers, interrupts, retries, limits
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Checkpointers and thread_id, MemorySaver versus Postgres, long-term stores, human-in-the-loop interrupt and resume, RetryPolicy, node timeouts and the recursion limit.
source: LangGraph docs (persistence, interrupts, errors); langgraph source for RetryPolicy and recursion defaults

questions.prompt: A node does: charge_card(); ok = interrupt('approve?'); return {'ok': ok}. The graph runs with a checkpointer until the interrupt, then you resume once with Command(resume=True). How many times in total is charge_card() executed?
questions.explanation: On resume LangGraph re-runs the interrupted node from its first line; interrupt() then returns the resume value instead of pausing. So the code before interrupt() runs twice (I counted it with a run). Put side effects after interrupt() or make them idempotent.

questions.prompt: An agent graph (START -> agent, agent -> tools, tools -> agent) never terminates because the model keeps requesting tools. You invoke it with recursion_limit = 10. How many LLM calls (agent node runs) happen before GraphRecursionError is raised?
questions.explanation: Each superstep is one node run and the limit caps them at 10: agent, tools, agent, tools ... so 5 agent runs and 5 tool runs. I ran this loop and saw GraphRecursionError after exactly 10 node executions.

questions.prompt: A node is added with retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=4, retry_on=ConnectionError) and it raises ConnectionError on every attempt. How many times is the node function executed?
questions.explanation: max_attempts includes the first attempt, so 1 try + 3 retries = 4 executions, then the error propagates. Back-off between attempts grows by backoff_factor up to max_interval.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: A graph compiled with a checkpointer must be invoked with a thread_id in config['configurable'].
questions.reason: The checkpointer stores state snapshots per thread, keyed by thread_id.

whys.a: Right: without a thread key the saver cannot decide where to read or write; I got a ValueError when I omitted it.
whys.b: R is exactly the reason, so b is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Use one thread_id per conversation (for example user id + session id). The same id continues the conversation; a new id starts from empty state.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: interrupt() only works when the graph was compiled with a checkpointer.
questions.reason: A paused run is resumed by invoking the graph again with Command(resume=...) and the same thread_id.

whys.a: R describes resuming, which is a consequence of persistence rather than the reason a checkpointer is required, so a is wrong.
whys.b: Both are true: the paused state must be saved somewhere, and resume locates it by thread_id; R is a related fact, not the direct explanation.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Without persistence there is nothing to resume from, because the process may even restart between the pause and the human reply.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: MemorySaver is meant for development and tests rather than production.
questions.reason: MemorySaver can store only one thread at a time.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so b is wrong.
whys.c: A is true (state lives in process memory and is lost on restart); R is false because it keeps many threads, which I confirmed with two thread ids.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: For production use a durable saver such as PostgresSaver (call setup() once) or the async variant, so state survives restarts and is shared between workers.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: After resuming, the node continues on the line following interrupt() without running its earlier lines again.
questions.reason: interrupt() returns the value supplied through Command(resume=...) when the node is re-run.

whys.a: A is false, so a is wrong.
whys.b: A is false, so b is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is false: the whole node restarts from the top; R is true and is how the answer reaches your code.

questions.explanation: Rules of thumb: keep nodes small, put interrupt() first, keep earlier code idempotent, and keep the order of multiple interrupts in a node stable.

questions.prompt: Match each persistence term with its meaning.

right.text: Snapshot of graph state saved after a superstep
In-process saver for development, lost on restart
Durable saver backed by a database, needs setup() once
Cap on node executions per run

questions.explanation: Checkpointers give short-term (per-thread) memory; a Store gives long-term memory such as user preferences across threads. recursion_limit is a run option, not persistence.

questions.text: Invoke with config={'configurable': {'{1}': 'user-42'}} and read the saved snapshot with app.{2}(config); its .next lists the nodes that still have to run.
questions.explanation: get_state_history lists all earlier checkpoints, which is how time travel and replay are done.

questions.text: A node pauses by calling {1}(value); the caller resumes with {2}(resume=answer) on the same thread, and the paused node restarts from its {3}.
questions.explanation: The pause payload appears under __interrupt__ in the result and in get_state(...).tasks.

questions.prompt: Compile the builder variable builder with an in-memory checkpointer into app, then invoke it twice with the inputs first and second on the same conversation 'u1'.
questions.model:
app = builder.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver())
cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "u1"}}
app.invoke(first, cfg)
app.invoke(second, cfg)
questions.explanation: InMemorySaver is the newer alias name of the same class. The second call continues from the state saved by the first because the thread id is the same.

questions.prompt: Write a node approve(state) that pauses with the payload {'action': state['action']} and stores the human's answer in the state key approved, then write the call that resumes the paused run with True using the variables app and cfg.

checks.label: calls interrupt with the action payload

questions.explanation: Other shapes pass (inline return, a variable for the answer). The resume call must use the same thread_id config, otherwise it starts nothing.

questions.prompt: Add a node 'call_api' (function call_api) to the builder variable g with a RetryPolicy of at most 5 attempts, a first back-off of 1 second, retrying only on ConnectionError.
questions.explanation: The default retry_on does not retry ValueError, TypeError or RuntimeError (I read the installed source), so list the exceptions you want. Also set a client-side timeout inside the node.

questions.prompt: With the variables DB_URI and builder, write the setup for the Postgres checkpointer: open it from the connection string as a context manager, create its tables, and compile the graph with it into app.

checks.label: opens PostgresSaver.from_conn_string(DB_URI) in a with block

questions.model:
with PostgresSaver.from_conn_string(DB_URI) as checkpointer:
    checkpointer.setup()
    app = builder.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)
questions.explanation: setup() runs the migrations and is needed once. Long-lived servers usually keep the saver open (connection pool) instead of leaving the with block. Async apps use AsyncPostgresSaver.

questions.prompt: A node raises RuntimeError('rate limited') and was added with retry_policy=RetryPolicy() using all defaults. In current LangGraph, what happens?

options.text: It is not retried, because the default retry_on skips ValueError, TypeError and RuntimeError.
options.why: Right: the default only retries connection errors, HTTP 5xx and unlisted exception types.

options.text: It is retried 3 times with exponential back-off, because every exception type counts for the default retry policy.
options.why: Not so: the default predicate excludes several built-in exception classes.

options.text: It is retried forever, until the recursion limit is hit, since no maximum attempt count is set.
options.why: max_attempts defaults to 3, and retries are separate from the recursion limit.

options.text: It is retried only if the node is async, because sync nodes are never retried by LangGraph.
options.why: Retry works for sync and async nodes alike; the exception type decides.

questions.explanation: Verified in langgraph source (default_retry_on). Be explicit with retry_on=(...) for rate limit and timeout errors of your SDK, which often subclass other exception types.

questions.prompt: Which statements about loop safety and timeouts in LangGraph are true? Select all that apply.

options.why: True: it is the safety net against endless agent loops.

options.text: A step counter in state, with a conditional edge to a fallback node, stops a loop before the hard limit.
options.why: True: this gives a graceful answer instead of an exception.

options.text: Recent releases raised the default recursion limit well above 25, so set recursion_limit explicitly.
options.why: True: I read 10007 as the default in langgraph 1.2; docs and older versions cite 25.

options.text: Raising recursion_limit is the correct fix for a loop that never terminates.
options.why: False: it only delays the failure and burns more tokens.

options.text: add_node(timeout=...) also cancels blocking synchronous nodes safely.
options.why: False: the docs say timeouts are supported only for async nodes.

questions.explanation: Set recursion_limit as a deliberate budget (for example 2 x the max tool rounds + 1), add a loop counter, and put HTTP/model timeouts on the clients themselves.
